text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

A survey of the results of 749 listed companies conducted by the Australian Financial Review and the Australian Stock Exchange found that core profitability, measured by earnings before interest and tax, was down 2.4 per cent in 1995-96. This is the worst profit reversal corporate Australia has faced since the recession. Page 1.

It is a third of the way through the crucial Budget session and the Federal Government is having to revise its legislative strategy in a bid to negotiate the passage of controversial reforms through a Senate chamber which it does not control, as key businss, economic and Budget reforms face major delays. Page 3.

A contentious draft tax ruling introduced in 1992, which discouraged companies from borrowing in Australia to buy assets overseas has been withdrawn, awaiting the result of a major court case on the issue. However many of the Australian multinationals looking to expand their international operations may still have trouble claiming interest on money borrowed, if there is a hint the money is being used to fund that overseas expansion. Page 4.

Two former high profile Sydney-based stockbrokers, Michael Whitworth and Robert Skinner, are to launch a new A$70 million investment fund today, which will invest entirely in cutting-edge US technology companies with capitalisation between less than A$632 million and up to US$2 billion, focusing on star performers ignored by the large US institutions and brokerage houses. Page 17.

The growing row between News Corporation and US cable-TV chief Ted Turner has dragged into its second week, with a counter-attack by News Corp's senior executive, vice-president and group general counsel Arthur Siskind to claims by the CNN boss that "Murdoch is like the late Fuhrer" Adolf Hitler and that journalists employed by News are told what to say. Page 19.

Coles Myer is expected to report a significant drop in profit today, with analysts predicting a net profit of between A$257 million and A$287 million, which is well down on the static A$423 million reported for 1994-95. The retailing giant delayed the announcement of its 1995-96 profit by two weeks, to allow its auditors more time to scrutinise the performance. Page 21.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Officials from the Group of Seven industrial nations have approved a debt-relief plan for as many as 20 of the world's poorest nations, involving the sale of about five million ounces of the International Monetary Fund's holdings of gold, while expressing satisfaction with overall prospects for the world economy. Page 17.

According to Australian Securities Commission chairman Alan Cameron, despite many disappointing results, disclosure and reporting standards were pleasingly high this reporting season. He said the results were no real surprise because companies had flagged the poor trading conditions beforehand. Page 17.

Financial markets are waiting with baited breath for the outcome of the Reserve Bank board meeting tomorrow, which will decide whether or not to drop interest rates. Economists are predicting that the release of retail trade and building approvals figures for August may persuade the RBA to cut short-term interest rates from seven per cent. Page 17.

CRA Ltd insiders have revealed there are concerns for the future of the company's A$200 million Ockley kaolin project in Western Australia due to intense competition in the global kaolin market and the technical requirements for processing the white clay roduct. A full feasibility study is expected to be considered next month. Page 17.

Following a recent Federal Government survey which showed Australia leads the world in known economic deposits of lead, mineral sands, silver, uranium, zinc and diamonds, AME Mineral Economics has revealed lead prices will continue to fall until 2000 and the outlook for zinc prices remains flat. Page 19.

Adding his voice to the growing number of industry insiders predicting the timing of a credit easing, Commonwealth Bank of Australia managing director David Murray said yesterday he wouldn't be surprised at all if the Reserve Bank moves to cut official interest rates tomorrow. Page 19.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Following a bitter price war, sugar industry rivals CSR, Mackay Refined Sugars and Manildra Harwood have held preliminary merger talks about rationalising the refined sugar industry, in a bid to overcome overcapacity and return to profits. However, the Australian Consumer and Competition Commission has revealed any merger would be closely scrutinised after its predecessor, the Trade Practices Commission, stopped a merger of Mackay with CSR three years ago. Page 35.

A 1992 controversial draft tax ruling, designed to restrict the deductibility of interest expenses related to the funding of overseas investments by Australian-based companies, has been withdrawn by the Australian Tax Office, pending the result of litigaton against Consolidated Press Holdings. Page 35.

One of Australia's most critical defence contracts, the Jindalee Over the Horizon Radar Network, could cost Telstra A$200 million due to delays, costs blow-outs and legal wrangles, even as speculation continues that the telecommunications carrier could belooking to sell its defence business before privatisation. Page 37.

MIM Holdings believes that its cost-cutting program will succeed in keeping the company in profit for the coming financial year, despite weaker copper prices and a stronger Australian dollar, but analysts have forecast a tough year ahead for the copper producer particularly at its Mount Isa operations. Page 37.

AME Mineral Economics has predicted that lead prices will fall by 15 per cent in real terms between 1996 and 2000, before recovering by 2005, while zinc will remain flat for the next decade, due to growing concern about environmental legislation and moves to lighter battery-powered vehicles. Page 37.

Commonwealth Bank chief executive David Murray claims there is a 50-50 chance that the Reserve Bank of Australia will cut interest rates this week, following the decision by the US Federal Reserve to hold rates steady. But he concedes there are two factor working against the rate cut - the RBA board doesn't often change rates on Tuesdays and secondly, it is rare for a 25 basis point cut. Page 37.
THE AGE

Microsoft Corporation has been forced to give free updates of its Chinese-language Windows 95, after users reported the appearance of anti-Communist slogans. Microsoft's Hong Kong spokesman Bryan Nelson said the rogue messages were contained in the software used for entering Chinese characters. Page C1.

Microsoft founder Bill Gates, the richest man in the world, had his salary boosted by 23 per cent this year, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, bringing his salary to US$340,618. Page C1.

Sugar rivals, CSR, Mackay Refined Sugars and Manildra Harwood have held preliminary merger talks with a view to overcoming the problem of overcapacity in the market and return to profits. Any merger would be closely scrutinised by the Australian Consumerand Competition Commission - the Trade Practices Commission torpedoed the refining merger of the two companies three years ago. Page C1.

Britain's Serious Fraud Office has begun a criminal probe of Peter Young, the fund manager sacked by Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, for hiding big stakes in risky unlisted securities in his portfolio. Page C3.

US Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said today Finance Ministers and central bankers of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations welcomed the recent strength of the dollar and reaffirmed their commitment to policies aimed at sustainable, non-inflationry growth. Page C3.

The Australian Taxation Office has withdrawn a controversial draft tax ruling, in place since 1992, pending the outcome of litigation it has taken against Kerry Packer's Consolidated Press Holdings. The ruling was designed to limit the deductibility of iterest expenses related to the funding of offshore investments by Australian resident companies. Page C3.
